explanation:
The `constexpr` specifier declares that it is possible for a function or variable to be evaluated at compile time. This allows the results of computations, including object construction and function calls, to be embedded directly into the program binary as constants, shifting work from runtime to compile time.

Scott Meyers' key insight is that `constexpr` fundamentally blurs the line between compile-time and run-time execution. It enables a powerful optimization strategy where complex initializations, traditionally performed when the program starts, can be resolved entirely by the compiler. This leads to faster-running applications, potentially at the cost of longer compilation times, by creating objects in read-only memory and pre-calculating values.

The mechanics are dual-purpose. When a `constexpr` function is invoked with arguments that are all compile-time constants, the compiler will attempt to evaluate the function and produce a compile-time constant result. If any argument is a runtime value, the same function code is compiled to execute at runtime like a normal function. For a class to participate, its constructor must be `constexpr`, and for an object to be fully compile-time, it must be declared `constexpr` and initialized with constant expressions.

This has significant practical implications. Objects created this way can be placed in read-only memory, which can be more efficient. The results from `constexpr` expressions can be used in contexts that demand compile-time constants, such as specifying array bounds, providing non-type template arguments, or defining enumerator values. This dramatically increases the scope of what can be defined as a true constant in C++.

A common pitfall is assuming `constexpr` guarantees compile-time evaluation. It only makes it *possible*. The function will run at runtime if its inputs are not compile-time constants. Another point of confusion is the set of limitations on what can be inside a `constexpr` function; while significantly relaxed in C++14 and later, not all C++ constructs are permitted in a compile-time context.
practical_example: A graphics application could pre-calculate a lookup table for a sine or cosine function at compile time. By using `constexpr`, the entire table can be computed by the compiler and stored in read-only memory, eliminating runtime initialization overhead and function call costs for lookups.
keywords: constexpr, compile time evaluation, constant expression, C++ compile time
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
